query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: In situ application of pulsed electric current during the solid‐state additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi will induce localized Joule heating and electromigration that accelerates dynamic recovery and dislocation annihilation, thereby reducing residual thermal stresses and preserving mechanical performance in miniature components.
generation.material_initial_state: Mechanically alloyed AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock with heterogeneous particle morphology and a potential for high thermal gradients during deposition.
generation.intervention: Integrate an electrode system into the deposition head and apply a controlled pulsed electric current concurrently with the deposition process.
generation.conditions: Process the miniature components under an inert atmosphere at an effective build-temperature window of approximately 300–400 °C. Use pulsed current parameters (e.g., pulse durations on the order of ~100 µs, at kilohertz frequencies, with optimized current density) during directed energy deposition.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced dynamic recovery resulting in accelerated dislocation mobility and annihilation at grain boundaries, yielding a more uniform, refined equiaxed grain structure.
generation.mechanism: The pulsed electric current generates localized Joule heating and induces electromigration forces that facilitate plastic relaxation. This in situ stimulation promotes dynamic recovery and reduces the accumulation of residual tensile stresses without resorting to high-temperature treatments that might otherwise degrade yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional high-thermal-load regimes, the treated components will exhibit a moderate to significant reduction in residual tensile stresses (e.g., potentially lowering stress levels by a comparable magnitude to in situ thermal management approaches) and a better retention of yield strength and ductility, while also simplifying process complexity by combining deposition and stress relief in one step.
generation.baseline: Miniature components manufactured under conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing conditions without the pulsed current intervention—resulting in higher residual stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and more complex post-processing requirements.
generation.boundary: This approach is anticipated to be effective for miniature, high-entropy alloy components where the geometry allows for efficient coupling of the pulsed current with the deposited material; its scalability to larger components may be limited by differences in thermal mass and cooling rates.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies (e.g., PMC11277587 and PMC7730888) support the benefits of in situ thermal management and surface stress modifications (using ultrasonic peening), the extension of these concepts into pulsed electric current intervention for AlCrFeNiSi is novel. Uncertainties include the optimal pulse parameters and the precise coupling between electromigration-induced atomic movements and residual stress relief in this specific alloy system.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components via the same solid-state additive manufacturing process. For the experimental group, apply the pulsed electric current during deposition using the prescribed pulse parameters; for the control group, process without any pulsed current intervention. Ensure identical deposition parameters (other than the pulsed current) and environmental controls. Post-fabrication, measure residual stresses and evaluate mechanical properties.
measurements: Residual stress distribution via X-ray diffraction and/or EBSD-based strain mapping
Grain structure and size via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)
Mechanical properties (yield strength, tensile strength, elongation) using miniature tensile testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental components show no statistically significant reduction in residual tensile stresses or if they exhibit degraded mechanical properties (e.g., reduced yield strength or ductility) compared to the control group, then the hypothesis that pulsed electric current in situ alleviates residual stresses without compromising performance will be falsified.

Metal additive manufacturing (AM) is a low-cost, high-efficiency functional mold manufacturing technology. However, when the functional section of the mold or part is not a partial area, and large-area additive processing of high-hardness metal is required, cracks occur frequently in AM and substrate materials owing to thermal stress and the accumulation of residual stresses. Hence, research on residual stress reduction technologies is required. In this study, we investigated the effect of reducing residual stress due to thermal deviation reduction using a real-time heating device as well as changes in laser power in the AM process for both high-hardness cold and hot work mold steel. The residual stress was measured using an X-ray stress diffraction device before and after AM. Compared to the AM processing conditions at room temperature (25 °C), residual stress decreased by 57% when the thermal deviation was reduced. The microstructures and mechanical properties of AM specimens manufactured under room-temperature and real-time preheating and heating conditions were analyzed using an optical microscope.
